title: Robinson Crusoe
author: Daniel Defoe
setting: York, the Barbary coast, Brazil, and an uninhabited island near the mouth of the Orinoco, between 1651 and 1687
lengthNote: Around 121,000 words; the familiar twenty chapters are an editorial convenience, since the first edition ran without them
openingLine: I was born in the year 1632, in the city of York, of a good family, though not of that country
summary: A young man who will not stay in the middle station of life is enslaved at Salé, prospers in Brazil, joins a voyage to buy Africans and is wrecked alone for twenty-eight years. Most of the book is work: salvage, fencing, baking, pottery, a canoe he cannot move to the water. Defoe makes an account-book out of a life, and the same habit that counts the goatskins also counts the mercies and calls the total Providence.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Robinson Crusoe
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription with modernised spelling. References give the chapter numbers of this reading text; the chapter division is editorial, since the 1719 edition prints the narrative continuously.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By William Taylor in London, presented as a life written by Crusoe himself.

atAGlance.label: Full first title
atAGlance.value: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
atAGlance.note: Defoe’s name appears nowhere on it; many first readers took the book for a genuine memoir.

atAGlance.label: Continuations
atAGlance.note: The Farther Adventures followed within months, and Serious Reflections in 1720.

atAGlance.label: Time on the island
atAGlance.note: From 30 September 1659 to 19 December 1686, by the reckoning Crusoe keeps on a post.

structure.label: Chapters I–III
structure.title: York, Salé and the Brazilian plantation
structure.summary: Crusoe leaves against his father’s advice, is wrecked within days of his first voyage and goes to sea again anyway. Captured by a Salé rover, he escapes in a boat with a boy called Xury, sells him to the Portuguese captain who rescues them both, and becomes a planter in Brazil. He is prosperous and bored when he agrees to fetch enslaved Africans from Guinea.

scenes.title: Start in Life
scenes.summary: The father’s argument for the middle station, the storm off Yarmouth, and the obstinacy that survives it.

scenes.title: Slavery and Escape
scenes.summary: Two years a slave at Salé, then a stolen boat, the African coast and a Portuguese ship bound for Brazil.

scenes.title: Wrecked on a Desert Island
scenes.summary: Xury is sold, the plantation thrives, and a voyage for slaves ends on a sandbank; Crusoe alone reaches the shore.

structure.label: Chapters IV–V
structure.title: The wreck, the raft and the dated record
structure.summary: Eleven trips to the wreck bring off tools, guns, powder, ink and money he laughs at and keeps. He builds a fortified dwelling, notches a post to hold the calendar, draws up a ledger of evil against good, and then starts the narrative again from the beginning in the form of a dated journal, so the same months are told twice at two distances.

scenes.title: First Weeks on the Island
scenes.summary: Salvage, the tent under the hill, and the balance sheet of comforts against miseries.

scenes.title: Builds a House — The Journal
scenes.summary: The dated journal opens on 30 September 1659 and runs until the ink begins to fail.

structure.label: Chapters VI–VIII
structure.title: Fever, tobacco and a Bible opened at random
structure.summary: An earthquake and then a long fever break the routine. Crusoe dreams of a figure with a flame about him, steeps tobacco in rum, opens a Bible at a verse about the day of trouble and dates his deliverance from that reading rather than from any rescue. The barley he first called a miracle is traced back to a bag he shook out himself.

scenes.title: Ill and Conscience-Stricken
scenes.summary: The fever, the dream, the tobacco cure and the first prayer he calls sincere.

scenes.title: Agricultural Experience
scenes.summary: Seasons learned by loss, seed hoarded, and a survey of the island that leaves him lord of all he sees.

scenes.title: Surveys His Position
scenes.summary: The calendar corrected, the Sabbath kept, and a settled comparison between this life and the one he led before.

structure.label: Chapters IX–X
structure.title: Work, failure and a second dwelling
structure.summary: The middle of the book is a record of processes: a canoe too heavy to launch, earthenware discovered by accident in the ashes, bread made from grinding to baking, goats tamed and penned. Defoe gives as much space to the failures as to the successes, which is what separates the whole novel from every abridgement of it.

scenes.title: A Boat
scenes.summary: A canoe hollowed out over months and left where it lies; the country house, the grapes, the parrot.

scenes.title: Tames Goats
scenes.summary: Pottery, a grindstone, a flock of his own, and a coasting voyage that nearly carries him out to sea for good.

structure.label: Chapters XI–XIII
structure.title: One footprint, and fifteen years of fear
structure.summary: A single print in the sand undoes twenty years of security. Crusoe fortifies, hides his goats, plans massacres and argues himself out of them on the ground that the cannibals have committed no crime against him. The chapters are a long study of what fear does to a man who has nobody to check his reasoning.

scenes.title: Finds Print of Man’s Foot on the Sand
scenes.summary: The print, the thunderstruck stop, and two years of broken sleep.

scenes.title: A Cave Retreat
scenes.summary: The bones on the shore, the plan to kill, and the argument that stops him.

scenes.title: Wreck of a Spanish Ship
scenes.summary: A second wreck, more salvage, and the wish for one companion that shapes the rest of the book.

structure.label: Chapters XIV–XVI
structure.title: Friday, and an island with subjects on it
structure.summary: Crusoe dreams of rescuing a prisoner who will serve him, and then does it. Friday is named for a date, taught to say Master before he is taught anything else, and converted — until he asks why God does not simply kill the devil. By the time a Spaniard and Friday’s father arrive, Crusoe is describing himself as lord and lawgiver of three subjects and three religions.

scenes.title: A Dream Realised
scenes.summary: The dream of a servant, the pursuit across the sand, and the token of submission Friday offers on the beach.

scenes.title: Friday’s Education
scenes.summary: Language, clothes, roast meat instead of human flesh, and a theological question Crusoe cannot answer.

scenes.title: Rescue of Prisoners from Cannibals
scenes.summary: The Spaniard and Friday’s father are saved; the island acquires a population and a constitution.

structure.label: Chapters XVII–XX
structure.title: The mutiny, the passage home and the reckoning
structure.summary: An English ship arrives with a captain and his officers about to be marooned by their own crew. Crusoe presents himself as the island’s governor, takes the ship, and sails after twenty-eight years to find that the Brazilian plantation has been making him rich in his absence. The last chapter crosses the Pyrenees in snow and ends with wolves, which is the book refusing to finish on the beach.

scenes.title: Visit of Mutineers
scenes.summary: Three men set ashore, the captain rescued, and a governor invented for the occasion.

scenes.title: The Ship Recovered
scenes.summary: The ship retaken, the ringleader hanged at the yardarm, and the worst of the mutineers left on the island in Crusoe’s place.

scenes.title: Return to England
scenes.summary: Lisbon, the old Portuguese captain, and an estate that has quietly accumulated for two decades.

scenes.title: Fight Between Friday and a Bear
scenes.summary: The overland journey through the Pyrenees, a wolf pack, and a promise of a second part.

characters.name: Robinson Crusoe
characters.role: Merchant, planter, slave, castaway, and self-appointed governor
characters.summary: A man who narrates his own life twice over: once as it happened and once as he later decides it should be understood. He is practical, repetitive and exhaustive about work, and equally exhaustive about accounting for his soul, using the same arithmetic of loss and gain for both.
characters.clue: He notches a post to keep the date, draws up his miseries and comforts in two columns like a ledger, and calls an island he never leaves for twenty-eight years his own property.

relationships.label: rescued and dealt fairly with by

characters.name: Crusoe’s father
characters.role: A merchant of Bremen settled at York
characters.summary: He appears for one speech and is quoted for the rest of the book. His case for the middle station — fewest disasters, fewest distempers, peace and plenty — is the standard against which Crusoe measures every subsequent calamity, usually while calling himself a warning to others.

characters.name: Xury
characters.role: A boy enslaved with Crusoe at Salé
characters.summary: He escapes with Crusoe, keeps watch through the nights on the African coast, offers to go ashore first and be shot first, and is sold within a chapter for sixty pieces of eight. Defoe records Crusoe’s reluctance and the terms of the sale in the same sentence, which is as close as the book comes to an admission.
characters.clue: He promises to be faithful and go all over the world with the man who then sells him to a Portuguese captain, with freedom offered in ten years if he turns Christian.

characters.name: The Portuguese captain
characters.role: The master who picks Crusoe up off the African coast
characters.summary: The one figure in the book who is repeatedly generous without calculation: he takes nothing for the passage, buys the boat at a price Crusoe does not set, and twenty years later hands over the Brazilian accounts to the penny. Defoe uses him as evidence that honest dealing is possible, and therefore that its absence elsewhere is a choice.

characters.name: Friday
characters.role: A prisoner rescued from cannibals on the shore
characters.summary: He is given a name from the calendar, taught the word Master before he is taught yes and no, and shown enormous affection within a relationship he never had the option of refusing. He is also the only character who asks Crusoe a question he cannot answer, and the book lets that stand.
characters.clue: Named after the day of his rescue, taught to call his rescuer Master, and the one person who asks why God does not simply kill the devil.

characters.name: Friday’s father
characters.role: An old prisoner saved from the canoe
characters.summary: His arrival turns the island from a household into a settlement and gives Friday the one relationship that is not owed to Crusoe. The reunion is the most straightforwardly felt scene in the book, and Crusoe reports it with some surprise at the strength of a feeling he has not arranged.

characters.name: The Spaniard
characters.role: A survivor of the wrecked ship, saved from the same canoe
characters.summary: He brings news that sixteen more of his countrymen are living on the mainland, and with him the island becomes a colonial question rather than a solitary one: who feeds them, who governs them, and on what terms they may be brought over. Crusoe draws up conditions before he will allow it.

characters.name: The English captain
characters.role: Master of the ship taken by mutineers
characters.summary: His arrival converts Crusoe’s private kingdom into something with a flag: the captain is told he is dealing with the governor, and the fiction is maintained through the whole recapture. He supplies the means of rescue and, in return, legitimacy for a claim Crusoe has been making to himself for years.

themes.name: Providence and interpretation
themes.summary: The book is less interested in whether God intervenes than in how Crusoe reads events. Barley springs up and is a miracle until he remembers the bag; an earthquake is a judgement until the fever supplies a better one. Defoe keeps the event, the first reading and the later reading visibly separate, so belief is shown being made rather than simply held.
themes.development: Warnings ignored in the storms of Chapters I–II, a conversion dated to a verse opened at random in Chapter VI, and a settled providential account of the whole life by Chapter XIV.

themes.name: Work and property
themes.summary: Crusoe turns survival into ownership: what he has made or fenced or fed becomes his, and the island follows. The novel gives unusual space to unsuccessful work — a canoe he cannot launch, a ruined first harvest, pots that collapse — so the claim to possession is built visibly out of hours rather than asserted.
themes.development: Salvage first, then manufacture, then agriculture and livestock; by Chapter IX he calls himself lord of the whole manor, and by Chapter XVI lord and lawgiver over people.

themes.name: Solitude and company
themes.summary: Twenty-four years pass before another human being is added, and the loneliness is described mostly through its substitutes: the parrot taught his own name, the dog at the table, the journal addressed to nobody. What Crusoe wants is not conversation but a servant, and the book grants that wish exactly.
themes.development: Comfort in routine, then terror at the footprint, then a dream of rescuing a man who will serve him — and the dream is what actually happens.

themes.name: Slavery, service and empire
themes.summary: Crusoe is enslaved at Salé, sells Xury, is wrecked on a voyage to buy Africans, and ends with three subjects of three religions and a fleet of settlers to place. The novel neither hides this sequence nor comments on it; the connections are all in the plot, waiting for a reader to make them.
themes.development: Slave in Chapter II, slave-trader in Chapter III, master in Chapter XIV, governor and proprietor by Chapter XVIII.

themes.name: Fear and its arithmetic
themes.summary: The footprint changes nothing material and everything else: the same island, the same stores, fifteen years of bad sleep. Defoe is precise about how fear reasons — it plans massacres, invents enemies, and then has to be argued down by an appeal to law and jurisdiction that Crusoe constructs himself.
themes.development: Storms and drowning at first, then the sea, then other people; the last fear is the ordinary one of losing the money he has accumulated by post.

themes.name: Keeping the account
themes.summary: Crusoe counts everything: days on a post, seeds, goats, pieces of eight, mercies against afflictions in two columns. The novel is written in the idiom of a merchant’s books, and it takes the form seriously enough to let the ink run out and the journal stop, which is a limit no spiritual autobiography would admit.
themes.development: The tally-post, the ledger of evil and good, the dated journal, and finally the Lisbon accounts that pay out eight-and-twenty years of profits.

techniques.name: Retrospective first person
techniques.definition: A narrator recounting his own past with the benefit of knowing how it ended.
techniques.inThisBook: Crusoe repeatedly corrects his younger self — what he then took for a miracle, what he now sees was a bag of chicken feed — so the book contains its own commentary.

techniques.name: The interpolated journal
techniques.definition: A dated record set inside a continuous narrative, covering ground the narrative has already told.
techniques.inThisBook: Chapter V begins the island story again from 30 September 1659 at a different distance, and the two accounts of the same months can be read against each other.

techniques.name: Circumstantial realism
techniques.definition: Conviction produced by the quantity and dullness of physical detail.
techniques.inThisBook: Eleven trips to the wreck, the exact list of what each raft carried, the months spent on a canoe that is never launched: the novel is persuasive because it is willing to be tedious.

techniques.name: Providential reading
techniques.definition: Treating events as a message and looking for what they are meant to teach.
techniques.inThisBook: A Bible opened at random supplies the date of his conversion, and thereafter every deliverance is entered on the credit side of a spiritual account.

techniques.name: Self-justification
techniques.definition: Reasoning conducted to license a course of action already wanted.
techniques.inThisBook: The argument that the cannibals have committed no crime against him stops a massacre; the same faculty finds no difficulty at all in the sale of Xury.

techniques.name: The inventory
techniques.definition: A list of goods used as narrative rather than as background.
techniques.inThisBook: Tools, powder, clothes, money and Bibles are counted off the wreck, and the running stock-take doubles as the measure of how far the island has been turned into an estate.

quotations.text: I was born in the year 1632, in the city of York, of a good family, though not of that country, my father being a foreigner of Bremen
quotations.context: The first sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: Year, city, family standing and the father’s country of origin, in that order: the opening is the form a deposition or a parish record takes, not the form a story takes. Defoe buys credit with it before a single event has happened, and many first readers spent it on believing the book was true.

quotations.text: the middle station of life was calculated for all kind of virtue and all kind of enjoyments; that peace and plenty were the handmaids of a middle fortune
quotations.context: Crusoe’s father arguing against a life at sea, in the one long speech he is given.
quotations.analysis: The father does not moralise; he makes an actuarial case, listing the distempers and vicissitudes that fall on the ranks above and below. The word ‘calculated’ gives the game away — virtue here is a matter of exposure and risk, and Crusoe spends the rest of the book proving his father’s figures right.

quotations.text: But my ill fate pushed me on now with an obstinacy that nothing could resist; and though I had several times loud calls from my reason and my more composed judgment to go home, yet I had no power to do it.
quotations.context: After the wreck off Yarmouth, going on to London by land rather than home to York.
quotations.analysis: He describes a compulsion and simultaneously reports that his reason was calling him home, so the sentence holds both explanations — fate, and a man choosing. Defoe uses that doubleness throughout: Crusoe is never so determined by Providence that he is not also answerable.

quotations.text: He offered me also sixty pieces of eight more for my boy Xury, which I was loth to take; not that I was unwilling to let the captain have him, but I was very loth to sell the poor boy’s liberty, who had assisted me so
quotations.context: The Portuguese captain’s offer, after the boy has spent weeks keeping watch on the African coast.
quotations.analysis: The reluctance and the price are in the same sentence, and the price wins. Crusoe records that he was loth to sell the boy’s liberty, which shows he knows exactly what is being sold; the transaction is entered in the narrative with the same care as the eighty pieces of eight for the boat.

quotations.text: he would give the boy an obligation to set him free in ten years, if he turned Christian: upon this, and Xury saying he was willing to go to him, I let the captain have him.
quotations.context: The terms on which Crusoe agrees to let the captain have Xury.
quotations.analysis: Conversion is made a condition of freedom, and the deal satisfies Crusoe’s conscience completely. Read this beside Friday, who is taught to say Master before he is taught yes and no: the book uses the same settlement twice and calls it kindness both times.

quotations.text: I stated very impartially, like debtor and creditor, the comforts I enjoyed against the miseries I suffered
quotations.context: Setting out his situation in two columns after the first weeks ashore.
quotations.analysis: The simile is not decorative: what follows is literally ruled into evil and good, item against item, cast off wretched against alive when the rest drowned. A merchant’s habit is applied to the state of a soul, and the comfort Crusoe draws from it comes from the form rather than from anything in the entries.

quotations.text: September 30, 1659⁠—I, poor miserable Robinson Crusoe, being shipwrecked during a dreadful storm in the offing, came on shore on this dismal, unfortunate island, which I called “The Island of Despair”; all the rest of the ship’s company being drowned, and myself almost dead.
quotations.context: The opening entry of the journal, written up later but dated to the day of the wreck.
quotations.analysis: The entry is dated to a day on which he had neither ink nor the heart to write, so the journal is a reconstruction pretending to be immediate. Naming the place is the first act of possession in the book, and the name he gives it will be quietly dropped as the island becomes an estate.

quotations.text: I began to suggest that God had miraculously caused His grain to grow without any help of seed sown, and that it was so directed purely for my sustenance on that wild, miserable place.
quotations.context: Finding green barley stalks growing near his fortification.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is careful — no seed was sown, therefore the cause is supernatural, therefore it is directed at him — and every step of it is sound except the first. Defoe shows a man deriving personal providence from an incomplete inventory of his own actions.

quotations.text: At last it occurred to my thoughts that I shook a bag of chickens’ meat out in that place; and then the wonder began to cease; and I must confess my religious thankfulness to God’s providence began to abate, too
quotations.context: Remembering, a little later, what he emptied out at that spot.
quotations.analysis: The correction is the most interesting sentence in the religious argument of the book, and Defoe lets Crusoe admit that his thankfulness abated with the wonder. Nothing is retracted — he goes on to say the hand of Providence was in it anyway — but the reader has now watched the machinery of a miracle being dismantled and rebuilt.

quotations.text: “Call on Me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify Me.”
quotations.context: The verse he lights on when he opens a Bible during the fever.
quotations.analysis: He opens the book casually, as he says, and the method is the one Betteredge uses with Robinson Crusoe itself in The Moonstone a century and a half later. Crusoe dates his deliverance from this reading rather than from any rescue, so the turning point of the novel is an act of interpretation.

quotations.text: I was king and lord of all this country indefensibly, and had a right of possession; and if I could convey it, I might have it in inheritance as completely as any lord of a manor in England.
quotations.context: Surveying the fertile side of the island for the first time.
quotations.analysis: Title, possession and inheritance arrive in one breath, and the legal vocabulary is exact: indefeasible right, conveyance, a manor in England. Crusoe cannot convey it to anybody and says so, which makes the claim a piece of pure form — ownership asserted because there is nobody present to dispute it.

quotations.text: how much more happy this life I now led was, with all its miserable circumstances, than the wicked, cursed, abominable life I led all the past part of my days
quotations.context: Reviewing his condition after the conversion, with the calendar and the Sabbath restored.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is between two lives and not two places, and it is the argument the whole island section rests on: solitude with belief is preferable to society without it. Defoe needs this settled before the footprint arrives, because everything after Chapter XI tests it.

quotations.text: I was lord of the whole manor; or, if I pleased, I might call myself king or emperor over the whole country which I had possession of: there were no rivals; I had no competitor, none to dispute sovereignty or command with me
quotations.context: Reflecting on how little his stores of corn and goats actually mean to him.
quotations.analysis: The passage climbs from manor to king to emperor and then collapses, because sovereignty with no rivals is indistinguishable from having nothing. Defoe puts the emptiness and the grandeur in the same sentence, and the reflection that follows — that he had nothing to covet — is the nearest the novel comes to contentment.

quotations.text: I was exceedingly surprised with the print of a man’s naked foot on the shore, which was very plain to be seen on the sand. I stood like one thunderstruck, or as if I had seen an apparition.
quotations.context: Walking towards his boat about noon, fifteen years into his stay.
quotations.analysis: Everything hangs on the singular: one print, and no others, which is why it cannot be explained and cannot be ignored. Defoe surrounds it with sober detail — about noon, very plain to be seen — and the effect of that plainness is the most frightening moment in eighteenth-century English fiction.

quotations.text: they were national, and I ought to leave them to the justice of God, who is the Governor of nations, and knows how, by national punishments, to make a just retribution for national offences
quotations.context: Arguing himself out of a plan to ambush and kill the cannibals.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is jurisdictional: these are national crimes, so they belong to a court he is not sitting in. It is the best moral thinking Crusoe does in the book, and it should be set against Chapter III, where the same faculty found no difficulty whatever in selling a boy.

quotations.text: I have been, in all my circumstances, a memento to those who are touched with the general plague of mankind, whence, for aught I know, one half of their miseries flow
quotations.context: Looking back over the whole course of his life from the settled island.
quotations.analysis: He offers himself as an exhibit, which is what a providential autobiography is supposed to do, and names the disease as discontent with one’s station. The claim sits oddly beside a narrator who is at that moment fortifying an island he has declared his own property.

quotations.text: kissed the ground, and laid his head upon the ground, and taking me by the foot, set my foot upon his head; this, it seems, was in token of swearing to be my slave forever.
quotations.context: On the shore, immediately after the rescue.
quotations.analysis: Crusoe reports the gesture and supplies its meaning in the same breath — ‘this, it seems’ — although he has no language in common with the man making it. The relationship is therefore interpreted into existence by the person it benefits, before a single word has been exchanged.

quotations.text: I let him know his name should be Friday, which was the day I saved his life; I called him so for the memory of the time. I likewise taught him to say “Master”; and then let him know that was to be my name
quotations.context: The first lesson, on the way back to the fortification.
quotations.analysis: A man is named after a date in Crusoe’s calendar, and the second word he is taught is the name of his owner; yes and no come afterwards. The order of instruction is the whole relationship, and Defoe sets it down without a syllable of comment.

quotations.text: if God much stronger, much might as the wicked devil, why God no kill the devil, so make him no more do wicked?”
quotations.context: Friday’s reply during a lesson on the devil and temptation.
quotations.analysis: The question is the oldest difficulty in Christian apologetics, put by a man who has been learning English for a few months, and Crusoe admits he was strangely surprised and ill qualified to answer. It is the only argument in the book that the narrator loses.

quotations.text: My island was now peopled, and I thought myself very rich in subjects; and it was a merry reflection, which I frequently made, how like a king I looked. First of all, the whole country was my own property, so that I had an undoubted right of dominion. Secondly, my people were perfectly subjected⁠—I was absolutely lord and lawgiver⁠—they all owed their lives to me, and were ready to lay down their lives, if there had been occasion for it, for me. It was remarkable, too, I had but three subjects, and they were of three different religions⁠—my man Friday was a Protestant, his father was a Pagan and a cannibal, and the Spaniard was a Papist. However, I allowed liberty of conscience throughout my dominions.
quotations.context: With Friday, Friday’s father and the Spaniard all on the island.
quotations.analysis: Three men become dominion, property and a constitutional settlement, complete with liberty of conscience granted from above to a Protestant, a pagan and a Catholic. The passage is offered as a merry reflection, and it is also a precise short description of how a colony describes itself.

quotations.text: And thus I left the island, the 19th of December, as I found by the ship’s account, in the year 1686, after I had been upon it eight-and-twenty years, two months, and nineteen days
quotations.context: Sailing at last, twenty-eight years after the wreck.
quotations.analysis: The great release of the book is given as an arithmetic result to the day, checked against the ship’s account rather than his own post. After a lifetime of counting, the final figure is the only celebration Crusoe permits himself.

timeline.label: Crusoe born at York
timeline.detail: The first sentence of the novel gives the year, the city and his father’s origins in Bremen.

timeline.label: He sails from Hull against his father’s advice
timeline.detail: Dated 1 September 1651 in the text, and wrecked off Yarmouth within days.

timeline.label: Wrecked on the island
timeline.detail: 30 September 1659, the date the journal opens on and the day notched at the head of the post.

timeline.label: Daniel Defoe born in London
timeline.detail: The son of a tallow chandler, educated for the Dissenting ministry and afterwards a merchant, bankrupt and pamphleteer.

timeline.label: Crusoe leaves the island
timeline.detail: 19 December 1686, after eight-and-twenty years, two months and nineteen days.

timeline.label: Defoe pilloried for The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
timeline.detail: A satire taken for the thing it imitated — an early demonstration of how completely he could disappear into a voice.

timeline.label: Alexander Selkirk is put ashore on Juan Fernández
timeline.detail: He was taken off in 1709; his case was widely reported and is the nearest thing the novel has to a documented source.

timeline.label: Robinson Crusoe published
timeline.detail: 25 April, by William Taylor, with no author’s name and a title page promising a life written by Crusoe himself.

timeline.label: The Farther Adventures follows
timeline.detail: Published in August of the same year, taking Crusoe back to the island and on to China and Siberia.

timeline.label: Serious Reflections During the Life of Robinson Crusoe
timeline.detail: A third volume of essays, in which the story is defended as an allegory of Defoe’s own life.

timeline.label: Defoe dies in Ropemaker’s Alley, London
timeline.detail: In lodgings, evading creditors, having written more than most of his contemporaries had read.

timeline.label: Rousseau makes it the one book in Émile’s library
timeline.detail: In Émile, Robinson Crusoe is recommended as the whole of a boy’s early reading — the beginning of its career as an educational text.

places.name: York
places.note: Crusoe’s birthplace, and the middle station of life he refuses.

places.name: Hull
places.note: Where he goes on board in September 1651 without his parents’ knowledge.

places.name: Yarmouth Roads
places.note: The anchorage where his first ship founders, and where he ignores the first warning.

places.name: Salé
places.note: The Moroccan port whose rovers take him; he is a slave there for two years.

places.name: Bahia, Brazil
places.note: Where he lands after his escape and builds the plantation that makes him rich in his absence.

places.name: Mouth of the Orinoco
places.note: The stretch of coast the island is placed off, which is why the canoes and the Spaniards come from the mainland.

places.name: Lisbon
places.note: Where the old Portuguese captain renders twenty-eight years of accounts to the penny.

criticalViews.summary: The book follows the Dissenting pattern exactly: a warning ignored, a career of disobedience, an affliction, a conversion dated to a text, and a life afterwards read backwards as Providence. On this account the island is a punishment that becomes a mercy.
criticalViews.counter: The form is there, but Defoe keeps showing the reading being constructed — the barley, the abating thankfulness — which a straightforward spiritual autobiography would not risk.

criticalViews.position: The first novel of economic man
criticalViews.summary: Crusoe measures his life in labour, stock and profit; the island is improved rather than merely survived, and the book’s realism is inseparable from its accounting. Much criticism since the 1950s has treated it as the founding text of the novel’s middle-class subject matter.
criticalViews.counter: It risks losing the religion, which is not decoration: Crusoe keeps two sets of books, and he takes the spiritual one at least as seriously.

criticalViews.summary: The plot moves from being enslaved to selling a boy to being wrecked on a slaving voyage to owning an island and granting its inhabitants liberty of conscience. The sequence is the novel’s own, and Friday’s first English word is Master.
criticalViews.counter: Reading it only as an apology for empire flattens the passages where Crusoe argues himself out of violence, and the book’s unusual willingness to record what the transactions cost.

essayQuestions.question: How does Defoe make an invented life convincing?
plan: Start with the opening sentence and what its order of information — year, city, family, origins — borrows from record-keeping.
Examine the inventories: eleven trips to the wreck, the goods on each raft, the money he mocks and keeps.
Show how failure earns belief: the canoe that cannot be launched, the first pots, the ruined sowing.
Read the journal as a deliberate formal risk, including the admission that the ink is running out.
Weigh the cost of the method: what a novel gives up in shapeliness to be believed.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Crusoe converts everything he touches into property.’ Discuss.
plan: Trace the sequence from salvage to manufacture to agriculture, and the point at which use becomes title.
Read the survey in Chapter VII, where he calls himself king and lord indefeasibly of land he cannot convey.
Set the reflection in Chapter IX — lord of the whole manor, with nothing to covet — against that claim.
Follow the logic into people: three subjects, three religions, liberty of conscience granted from above.
Decide whether the novel endorses the process or simply records it with unusual completeness.

essayQuestions.question: What part does Providence play in the novel, and how far does Crusoe make it himself?
plan: Distinguish the event, Crusoe’s first reading of it, and the reading he settles on later.
Use the barley and the shaken bag as the clearest case, including the abating thankfulness.
Examine the conversion in Chapter VI: a fever, a dream, tobacco, and a Bible opened casually.
Consider the warnings of Chapters I and II, which are only warnings once the outcome is known.
Conclude on what the novel shows about how a providential account of a life gets written.

essayQuestions.question: How should a reader today handle the novel’s treatment of Xury and Friday?
essayQuestions.focus: Slavery, service and the book’s silences
plan: Set out the plot facts in order: enslaved at Salé, sells Xury, wrecked on a slaving voyage, acquires Friday.
Read the sale of Xury closely, noting that Crusoe records his own reluctance and the price in one sentence.
Examine the order in which Friday is taught English, and what the first two words establish.
Give full weight to Friday’s question about the devil, the one argument Crusoe admits he cannot answer.
Judge how far the novel is aware of the pattern it lays out, and whether awareness would change the reckoning.

discussionQuestions: Defoe spends whole chapters on baking bread and firing pots. What would be lost if they were cut, as they usually are?
Crusoe remembers the bag of chicken feed and his thankfulness abates. Does the novel believe in Providence or in Crusoe’s need for it?
One footprint frightens him for fifteen years. Why is a single print more disturbing than a crowd would be?
Friday is named for a day and taught ‘Master’ before ‘yes’. How much does Defoe see of what he has written down?
The book does not end when the ship arrives; it ends with wolves in the Pyrenees. What is that last chapter for?

related.why: The satirical answer to it, published seven years later and wearing the same documentary clothes.
Betteredge treats Robinson Crusoe as an oracle, opening it at random for guidance — one foundational English story used inside another.
An earlier first-person account from the plantations, and a direct view of what Crusoe’s Guinea voyage was for.
The other great novel of work at sea, equally willing to stop the story to explain a process in full.
The next decade’s experiment in making fiction out of a plain private record, and another book that persuaded readers it was real.
